En el tema de [[al-matrices|matrices]] e: In the topic on [[al-matrices|matrices]] the determinant appeared as a calculation: $ad - bc$ for order 2 and Sarrus' rule for order 3. Here it becomes a tool. First, its properties, which let you calculate without doing all the arithmetic and guess the result at a glance. Then, cofactor expansion, which works for matrices of any size. And at the end, the rank, which is what is really used to discuss systems and the relative positions of lines and planes.

El desarrollo por menores lo publicó Pie: Expansion by minors was published by Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1772, inside a work on the orbits of the planets: he needed to solve systems of equations and was after a general way of writing their solutions. The word determinant in its present sense is due to Augustin Cauchy, in 1812, who was the one who proved that the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants. Matrices, as an object with a name of their own, did not arrive until 1858: for almost a century determinants were worked out for tables of numbers nobody had granted any standing.
El <strong>rango</strong> de una matriz: The rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows, that is, how many rows are left that cannot be obtained by combining the others. It is the same number if you count columns. It is worked out in two ways, and it pays to master both:
<strong>Por Gauss</strong>: se escalona: By Gauss: you put the matrix in echelon form and count the rows that do not end up entirely zero.
<strong>Por menores</strong>: el rango e: By minors: the rank is the order of the largest non-zero minor. You look for a non-zero 2×2 minor and go on “bordering” it (adding a row and a column) to see whether there is a non-zero 3×3 one.
\\operatorname{rg}(A) = r \\iff \\text{h: \operatorname{rank}(A) = r \iff \text{there is a non-zero minor of order } r \text{ and all those of order } r+1 \text{ are zero}

$\operatorname{rank}(A)$ is read “rank of A”.

In practice: if a 3×3 matrix has a non-zero determinant, its rank is 3 with no further work. If it is zero, the rank is at most 2, and finding one non-zero 2×2 minor is enough to make sure it is exactly 2.

Olga Taussky-Todd, una matemática nacida: Olga Taussky-Todd, a mathematician born in Olomouc in 1906, came to matrices through a life-or-death problem. During the Second World War she worked at the British National Physical Laboratory studying flutter: the vibration that can tear the wings off an aircraft at a certain speed. Deciding whether a design was safe meant studying enormous matrices, and she found ways to bound their properties without working everything out. Later, in the United States, she became one of the great champions of matrix theory as a discipline in its own right.
El determinante mide cuánto estira o enc: The determinant measures how much a transformation stretches or shrinks space, and that is why it turns up in an unexpected place: when changing variables in a multi-dimensional integral, the determinant (the Jacobian) is the factor that corrects the areas and volumes. And the rank is the check an engineering program makes before solving an enormous system: if the matrix of a structure does not have full rank, the structure is a mechanism and moves on its own, that is, it falls down.
